guide: Start at the East Quay before the fishing boats head back out, then follow the painted seawall toward the old net sheds. The small bakery on Lantern Lane is good for a warm roll and coffee; ask what came out of the oven that morning. For lunch, choose a chalkboard seafood special at one of the family-run rooms near the ferry steps. The pier gets windy, so bring a light layer even on a bright day.

Walk uphill from the ferry landing to the slate-roofed watch houses on Beacon Row, then continue to the signal tower for a view across the inlet. The old ropewalk has been turned into workshops, and its long brick walls make a useful route marker through the west quarter. Take the steep lanes slowly; several are cobbled and the public steps can be slick after rain.

At low tide, follow the boardwalk east from Saltmarsh Gate to watch wading birds feed in the shallow pools. Keep to the marked path so the nesting grass stays undisturbed, and bring binoculars if you have them. Late afternoon gives the reed beds a soft gold edge. The path is exposed, so check the local tide board before setting out and carry water.

The Saturday market gathers under the blue awnings at Foundry Square. Pick up smoked mussels, rye cakes, or seasonal fruit for a picnic by the water, and ask the stallholders which boats brought in the day's catch. Afterward, browse the independent makers along Rope Lane. Market days can shift around holidays, so confirm the schedule with the visitor desk.

For a rainy spell, browse the secondhand shelves at Gull & Quill on Rope Lane, then settle into the window seats at the adjoining tea room. The harbor history room in the former customs house is small enough to enjoy without rushing and gives context to the quay outside. Bring a compact umbrella; sea showers tend to pass quickly, but the lanes stay damp.

Rent a bicycle near the ferry landing and take the signed coast path west to Alder Point. The route passes a disused lighthouse keeper's garden and several sheltered coves; lock your bike before walking down to the beach. Pack lunch from the market and refill your bottle in the village square before leaving, since services are sparse along the headland.

On some weekends, musicians play in the upper room of the Anchor Hall, a former chandlery above the west quay. Ask at the harbor visitor desk what is happening during your stay, then have an early supper on Lantern Lane before the walk over. The harbor path is dim after dusk, so use the lit streets back toward the ferry square.

A gentle outing starts at the ferry steps, where you can watch small workboats come and go, then loops through the level waterfront garden to the maritime shed. The shed has model boats and simple activities for younger visitors. Bring snacks and take breaks at the benches along the quay; the upper town is much steeper if you decide to explore farther.
